title: Technology-Assisted Review in E-Discovery Can Be More Effective and More Efficient Than Exhaustive Manual Review
pub: Richmond Journal of Law & Technology, vol. XVII, issue 3
author: Maura R. Grossman · Gordon V. Cormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s selective, human-led deployment model and materially strengthens it with controlled evidence that an interactive human–computer workflow can outperform exhaustive manual review on a bounded legal task while using far less human effort. Its caveats about process quality, metric trade-offs and study selection also reinforce task-specific evaluation rather than general claims of autonomous legal competence.
qs: As such, the results support the conclusion that technology-assisted review can achieve at least as high recall as manual review, and higher precision, at a fraction of the review effort, and hence, a fraction of the cost.
The particular processes found to be superior in this study are both interactive, employing a combination of computer and human input.

st.t: E-discovery evidence: Manual review is no gold standard
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: two tested human–computer review processes achieved stronger retrieval performance with substantially less document examination than estimated exhaustive manual review. It also aligns with the cluster’s constraints by retaining human judgment, relying on statistical inference and an adjudicated relevance standard, and acknowledging simulation and Enron-familiarity limits rather than claiming universal machine superiority.

st.t: Predictive coding: Mature automation still needs transparency
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that technology-assisted review reduces exhaustive human review through selective human coding and automated classification, while evidence challenges manual review’s assumed superiority without establishing universally superior accuracy. Its cited debate over comparative efficacy reinforces the cluster’s qualified, evidence-sensitive framing.
qs: at 194 (“The comparative efficacy of the results of manual review versus the results of alternative forms of automated methods of review remains very much an open matter of debate.”).

st.t: TAR governance: Reduced review retains legal judgment
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition: selected interactive human–computer review processes substantially reduced human review while retaining human input. Its process-specific findings and qualifications on recall, team selection and the inferred manual-review baseline also align with the synthesis’s caution against universal algorithmic superiority.
qs: The particular processes found to be superior in this study are both interactive, employing a combination of computer and human input.
The technology-assisted reviews require, on average, human review of only 1.9% of the documents, a fifty-fold savings over exhaustive manual review.

kp.k: Technology-assisted review can outperform exhaustive manual review
kp.d: Grossman and Cormack analyse the TREC 2009 Legal Track Interactive Task to challenge the assumption that exhaustive human review is the most effective and defensible approach to e-discovery. Their finding concerns two particular interactive human–computer processes, not every technology-assisted system or autonomous replacement of legal judgment.
qs: Technology-assisted review can (and does) yield more accurate results than exhaustive manual review, with much lower effort.
Of course, not all technology-assisted reviews (and not all manual reviews) are created equal.
While these processes require the review of orders of magnitude fewer documents than exhaustive manual review, neither entails the naïve application of technology absent human judgment.

kp.k: Automation changes document selection and classification work
kp.d: The authors define technology-assisted review as an interplay of humans and computers for identifying responsive or privileged documents. Humans review selected documents rather than necessarily examining the entire collection; technology can use those judgments to classify or rank other documents. Listed approaches include keyword and Boolean search, conceptual search, clustering, machine learning, relevance ranking and sampling.
qs: A technology-assisted review process involves the interplay of humans and computers to identify the documents in a collection that are responsive to a production request, or to identify those documents that should be withheld on the basis of privilege.
Using the results of this human review, the computer codes the remaining documents in the collection for responsiveness (or privilege).

kp.k: Discovery obligations balance completeness against proportionality
kp.d: Using the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure discussed in this 2011 article, the authors frame document review as a tension between completeness and burden or cost. They identify manual review as the dominant e-discovery cost and ask whether it is the most effective and efficient means of finding the information needed to resolve disputes. The empirical comparison informs that question rather than establishing a judicial ruling endorsing particular technologies.
qs: Together, Rules 26(g)(1), 26(b)(2)(C)(iii), and 37(a)(4) reflect the tension – between completeness on one hand, and burden and cost on the other – that exists in all electronic discovery (“e-discovery”) processes.

In current practice, the problem of identifying responsive (or privileged) ESI, once it has been collected, is almost always addressed, at least in part, by a manual review process, the cost of which dominates the e-discovery process.

kp.k: Human disagreement undermines manual review's gold-standard status
kp.d: The authors report substantial disagreement in earlier information-retrieval and legal-review studies. Voorhees found assessor overlap of 42.1%, 49.4% and 42.6%. Grossman and Cormack calculate overlap of 16.3% and 15.8% between two subsequent legal-review teams and an original DOJ production, and 28.1% between those teams. They distinguish overlap from accuracy: disagreement alone cannot establish which reviewer is correct.
qs: It is well established that human assessors will disagree in a substantial number of cases as to whether a document is relevant, regardless of the information need or the assessors’ expertise and diligence.
Measurements of overlap provide little information regarding the accuracy of particular assessors because there is no “gold standard” against which to compare them.

kp.k: Prior studies expose unreliable search confidence and evaluation
kp.d: The article reports that Blair and Maron's paralegal searchers believed they had retrieved 75% of relevant documents across 51 requests, but achieved average recall of 20.0% and precision of 79.0%; Grossman and Cormack calculate average F1 of 28.0%. Separately, they regard the Roitblat, Kershaw and Oot comparison as inconclusive because changing its gold standard altered measured performance far more than the apparent technology advantage.
qs: Although the searchers believed they had found 75% of the relevant documents, their average recall was only 20.0%.
However, due to the use of the alternate gold standard, the result is inconclusive.

kp.k: TREC comparison uses common tasks and adjudicated assessments
kp.d: TREC 2009 used 836,165 Enron email messages and attachments, a mock complaint and seven production requests. This study compares H5's one submission and Waterloo's four submissions with contemporaneous first-pass manual assessments on stratified samples of about 7,000 documents per topic. Senior-attorney Topic Authorities adjudicated appealed assessments; unappealed first-pass decisions remained in the gold standard. Exhaustive manual-review performance was statistically estimated, not observed through an actual review of every document.
qs: In comparing the manual and technology-assisted reviews, the Authors used exactly the same adjudicated gold standard as TREC.

The manual reviews considered for this Article were the “First- Pass Assessments” undertaken at the request of the TREC coordinators for the purpose of evaluating the participating teams’ submissions.

kp.k: Precision and overall effectiveness improve significantly
kp.d: Across five topics, technology-assisted review averaged 76.7% recall, 84.7% precision and 80.0% F1, compared with manual review's 59.3%, 31.7% and 36.0%. Average precision and F1 advantages were overwhelmingly statistically significant (P < 0.001); the average recall advantage was not significant (P > 0.1). Four topics showed significantly higher technology-assisted F1; Topic 207 showed no meaningful difference on any measure. Manual review was not significantly better on any measure.
qs: For F1 and precision, the measured difference is overwhelmingly statistically significant (P < 0.001);
The measurements also suggest that the technology-assisted processes may yield better recall, but the statistical evidence is insufficiently strong to support a firm conclusion to this effect.
There is not one single measure for which manual review is significantly better than technology-assisted review.

kp.d: The five technology-assisted efforts reviewed between 4,369 and 34,446 documents per topic, or 0.5%–4.1% of the collection. Average human review covered 1.9% of documents, which the authors describe as a fifty-fold saving against exhaustive review. This efficiency comparison principally measures document counts, not a complete monetary-cost comparison; H5 did not disclose person-hours.
qs: The technology-assisted reviews require, on average, human review of only 1.9% of the documents, a fifty-fold savings over exhaustive manual review.
H5 declined to quantify the number of person-hours

kp.k: H5 combines relevance definition, precise queries and measurement
kp.d: H5's reported method iteratively defines relevance, designs deterministic queries and measures precision and recall. Rather than relying on a few broad keywords, it develops many precise queries whose combined results aim to capture most relevant documents. H5 reviewed 20,000 documents for Topic 204 and achieved 76.2% recall, 84.4% precision and 80.1% F1. These methodological descriptions are attributed to H5, while performance figures come from the TREC analysis.
qs: According to Dan Brassil of H5, the H5 process involves three steps: (i) “definition of relevance,” (ii) “partly-automated design of deterministic queries,” and (iii) “measurement of precision and recall.”
In the course of its TREC 2009 effort, H5 sampled and reviewed a total of 20,000 documents.

kp.k: Waterloo accelerates review through active learning
kp.d: Waterloo combined interactive search and judging, active learning originally developed for spam filtering, and recall estimation. Across four topics, approximately 12,500 documents were reviewed during search at about three per minute, followed by approximately 50,000 during active learning at 20 per minute. Total review time was about 118 hours, averaging 30 hours per topic. Crucially, every produced document received human review; the system reduced the population needing examination rather than directly producing unchecked documents.
qs: Waterloo’s approach consisted of three phases: (i) “interactive search and judging,” (ii) “active learning,” and (iii) recall estimation.
For Waterloo’s TREC 2009 effort, the end result was that a human reviewed every document produced;
Total review time for all phases was about 118 hours; 30 hours per topic, on average.

kp.k: Most examined human misses were not borderline judgments
kp.d: The authors qualitatively examined 211 documents on Topics 204 and 207 that professional manual reviewers marked nonresponsive but the technology-assisted teams and Topic Authorities deemed responsive. They classified 137 as inarguable errors, 67 as interpretive errors and seven as arguable errors, reporting fractions of 65%, 31% and 4%. These are the authors' judgments about a selected set of missed documents, not a classification of every error across the study.
qs: The vast majority of missed documents are attributable either to inarguable error or to misinterpretation of the definition of relevance (interpretive error).
Remarkably, the findings identify only 4% of all errors as arguable.

kp.k: Performance depends on the chosen review objective
kp.d: TREC participants were instructed to maximize F1, the harmonic mean of recall and precision, rather than recall alone. The authors suggest that prioritizing recall could lead participants to broaden relevance criteria or adjust software sensitivity, potentially sacrificing precision and F1. That alternative outcome is a possibility discussed by the authors, not a tested finding of this study.
qs: It should be noted that the objective of TREC participants was to maximize F1, not recall or precision, per se.

Had the participants considered recall to be more important, they might have traded off precision (and possibly F1) for recall, by using a broader interpretation of relevance, or by adjusting a sensitivity parameter in their software.

kp.d: The authors acknowledge a simulated litigation setting, possible prior familiarity with Enron, sampling uncertainty, and an appeal-dependent gold standard. Manual reviewers received more detailed guidance and reviewed samples richer in relevant documents than the full collection; the authors suggest these conditions may overestimate exhaustive manual-review effectiveness, but do not establish that effect empirically. Unappealed shared errors could inflate both methods' scores.
qs: Both participants and TAs may have had prior knowledge of both the story and dataset, affecting their strategies and assessments.
Beyond the statistical uncertainty, there also is uncertainty as to whether manual reviewers would have had the same error rate had they reviewed the entire collection.
The impact of the resulting errors on the gold standard would be to overstate both recall and precision for manual review, as well as for technology-assisted review, with no net advantage to either.

kp.k: Selected successful teams demonstrate possibility, not universal superiority
kp.d: The authors deliberately selected two of eleven TREC 2009 teams because they were most likely to demonstrate improvement over exhaustive manual review. Their five submissions were the most effective for their respective topics; Topics 205 and 206 were excluded because neither team submitted results. The authors applied a Bonferroni correction multiplying P by 11 and report that significance persisted. The resulting claim is that technology-assisted review can outperform manual review, not that typical implementations invariably do.
qs: In designing this study, the Authors considered only the results of two of the eleven teams participating in TREC 2009, because they were considered most likely to demonstrate that technology-assisted review can improve upon exhaustive manual review.
Even under Bonferroni correction, the results are overwhelmingly significant.
Future work may address which technology-assisted review process(es) will improve most on manual review, not whether technology- assisted review can improve on manual review.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Grossman and Cormack claim that interactive technology-assisted review can make e-discovery more accurate and substantially less labour-intensive than exhaustive manual review.
pts.d: The authors present this as a demonstrated capability of particular human–computer workflows, not a prediction that all legal AI will outperform lawyers. Across the five studied reviews, technology-assisted review achieved average precision of 84.7% versus 31.7% for manual review, and average F1 of 80.0% versus 36.0%. These differences were statistically significant. Average recall was 76.7% versus 59.3%, but that difference was not statistically significant. Technology-assisted review required humans to examine an average of 1.9% of the collection, described as a fifty-fold saving in document-review effort. The authors infer cost savings from reduced review effort; they do not report a comprehensive monetary cost comparison. The technologies include deterministic queries, search, sampling and active learning, rather than generative AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is the authors’ comparative statistical analysis of five H5 and Waterloo efforts in the TREC 2009 Legal Track Interactive Task.
pts.d: The task used mock production requests and 836,165 real Enron email messages and attachments. H5 completed one topic using an iterative query-design and measurement process; Waterloo completed four using interactive search, active learning and recall estimation. Humans reviewed 0.5%–4.1% of the collection per topic. The manual comparator consisted of first-pass assessments of stratified samples by law students or professional lawyer reviewers, extrapolated statistically to an exhaustive review; it was not an actual manual review of the entire collection. Both approaches were evaluated against the same adjudicated TREC gold standard, with senior-attorney Topic Authorities deciding appealed assessments. Precision and F1 differences favoured technology-assisted review significantly on four topics; Topic 207 showed no significant effectiveness difference. A qualitative examination of 211 documents missed by professional reviewers on two topics classified 65% as inarguable errors, 31% as interpretive errors and 4% as arguable errors. These classifications were the authors’ judgments.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2011 article reports capabilities demonstrated in 2009, conditional on the particular interactive workflows and experimental setting; it gives no adoption or displacement timetable.
pts.d: The authors explicitly limit their conclusion to the possibility of outperforming manual review, rather than universal superiority. They selected two of eleven teams knowing their submissions were the most effective for their respective topics, and report that significance survived a Bonferroni correction. Other qualifications include the simulated litigation setting, possible prior familiarity with Enron, extrapolation from enriched document samples, and a gold standard that reconsidered only appealed judgments. Participants aimed to maximise F1 rather than recall; prioritising recall could change the precision–recall trade-off. Human judgment remained integral. Waterloo's process included human review of every produced document, while avoiding review of most of the collection. H5 did not disclose total person-hours, so document counts should not be treated as a complete measurement of total labour or cost.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects concern civil-litigation document reviewers, supervising lawyers, litigants and courts balancing discovery completeness against burden and expense.
pts.d: For document-review teams, the claimed change is a reduction in the number of documents humans must examine, with computers helping select, rank or classify material and human judgment guiding the process. For supervising lawyers and litigants, the proposed benefit is more accurate production at reduced review effort and inferred cost. For courts and parties, the findings challenge treating exhaustive manual review as inherently the most effective or defensible method when assessing reasonable and proportional discovery. The authors do not establish job losses, changes in law-firm staffing structures, market-share shifts or broader replacement of legal advice. Although their general definition of technology-assisted review includes privilege identification, the central comparative results concern responsiveness to the studied production requests.
